prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world the agent's observation shows the target shifted: the target, missing, extra and target-height channels are rolled 4 rows toward higher y, wrapping around. The world, its designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials in this search yet. The starting network scores 0. Across past searches only one network family scored above 0. It feeds the legal-action mask, reshaped to [types, Y, X], in as input under four layouts (as given, transposed, y-flipped, x-flipped). It reads placement logits out through per-type maps re-laid in those same four layouts. Past searches suggest each world breaks its description in a different way, likely in how action indices map to cells. Recipe-only changes always gave 0. Round 1 therefore rebuilds that family as a baseline. It also tests one wider hedge, all 8 symmetries of the square for both mask input and logit output, and one recipe change on the rebuilt family: 2 PPO epochs, which gives about 1.8x more environment steps. A nonzero late-training success is the first real signal. Zeros on both seeds would mean the world breaks its description in some other way.

### Round 2
Only r1c1 (the 4-layout mask net) shows any signal: one seed reached 0.002 dev and late training success was 0.0016. That is essentially zero and within noise of r1c2 (8 dihedral layouts) and r1c3 (2 PPO epochs), which both scored 0. So this world breaks its description in a way that flips and transposes alone do not cover. The learned 1x1 stem already absorbs any permutation of observation channels, and per-type maps absorb any permutation of brick types. Two deviations remain untested. First, the action index may interleave types (cell-major, type-minor). Second, the DONE action may sit at another index, or stopping may need global context: a wrong stop time ruins exact builds even when every placement is correct. The recipe is not the bottleneck while success is 0. This round tests the type-minor layouts, a global per-action head, and both together with all 8 dihedral layouts.

### Round 3
Five of the six trials scored exactly 0. The one exception, r1c1, built 1 of 512 dev designs (0.002) on one seed and had a late training success of 0.0016. That is at noise level, but it is still the only training signal so far. These hedges all failed: 8 dihedral layouts, type-minor (cell-major) indexing, more samples with 2 PPO epochs, and a dense global per-action head. The dense head could in principle have learned a DONE action moved to another index, such as an off-by-one shift, so that explanation is now less likely. The fault is probably not one of the action-index permutations we covered. Two families remain untested. First, the observation channel groups may be spatially misaligned with each other, for example the target flipped or transposed relative to the build. Second, the network may be too weak at placing the right brick in the right order. Next I will refine r1c1 with a footprint-aware head in the action frame and with longer credit assignment, and add a hedge that feeds the observation in under several spatial transforms.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored about 0. Only r1c1, the plain 4-layout mask family, showed anything: one seed at 0.002 dev and 0.0016 training success. Two seeds can't tell that apart from zero. Wider layout hedges (8 dihedral, 16 with type order), a dihedral copy of the observation, footprint pooling heads, global action terms, fewer PPO epochs and longer credit assignment all gave exactly 0. So a layout deviation is probably not the main obstacle here. This world seems either harder to learn or broken in a way we can't see. With one round left, I keep the r1c1 family and try three different ways to improve it: (1) more frequent, larger-minibatch updates at about the same compute; (2) a trunk shared across layers and conditioned on the layer index, scoring each candidate landing layer, combined with the 4-layout hedge (earlier per-layer heads never had it); (3) a separate DONE detector reading the raw observation, because an exact build needs a well-timed stop.

## Trial it ended with
name: mask4-layout baseline
hypothesis: This rebuilds the only family that scored above 0. The legal mask goes in under 4 index layouts plus coordinates, followed by a 1x1 stem and a residual 3x3 trunk. Per-type logit maps are re-laid in the same 4 layouts and summed, so the network can learn how this world maps action indices to cells. I expect a dev score of at least 0.1. If both seeds score 0, this world breaks its description beyond flips and transposes.

Return a JSON object: "verdict" ("yes", "partly" or "no") and "evidence" (at most 80 words, quoting the text and
naming the round it comes from).

reply.evidence: Round 3 raises the right kind of change only as an untested candidate: "the observation channel groups may be spatially misaligned with each other, for example the target flipped or transposed relative to the build." This points to a spatial misalignment of the target relative to the build. But it never names the actual specifics: the target channels shifted 4 rows toward higher y, with wrap-around. Its examples (flip or transpose) are wrong, and Round 4 drops the idea.
